name: Leadership Qualities for the IT Industry
blurb: Leadership theories, organizational behaviour, groups & teams, culture, communication

questions.q: According to Keith Davis, leadership is:
options: The right to issue orders based on hierarchy
The ability to persuade others to seek defined objectives enthusiastically
The process of writing company policies
questions.explanation: Keith Davis defines leadership as the ability to persuade others to seek defined objectives enthusiastically — the human factor that binds and motivates a group.

questions.q: The 'Great Man' theory of leadership is based on the belief that:
options: Great leaders are born (often from aristocracy) and arise in times of need
Leadership depends entirely on the situation
Anyone can lead with the right rewards
questions.explanation: The Great Man theory holds that leaders are born great (historically often from aristocracy) and emerge in times of need.

questions.q: Servant-leadership theory is characterised by:
options: A shared-power system that puts the needs of others first and emphasises collaboration, trust and empathy
Decisions made only at the top
questions.explanation: Servant-leadership uses shared power, putting others' needs first and emphasising collaboration, trust, empathy and ethical power usage — the leader is a servant first.

questions.q: A leader who feels they must control every aspect of a project and won't delegate is falling into which trap?
questions.explanation: Micromanaging stems from a need to control every aspect; it stifles innovation and demotivates employees who fear their work will be changed or invalidated.

questions.q: Kirkpatrick and Locke identified six traits that differentiate leaders from non-leaders. Which is one of them?
questions.explanation: Kirkpatrick and Locke's six traits are Drive, Leadership motivation, Honesty/Integrity, Self-confidence, Cognitive ability and Knowledge of the business.

questions.q: Which five leadership traits consistently reappear across the major trait studies (Stogdill, Mann, etc.)?
options: Intelligence, self-confidence, determination, integrity and sociability
questions.explanation: Northouse summarises the five consistently-appearing traits as intelligence, self-confidence, determination, integrity and sociability.

questions.q: Which early thinker, in 'The Prince', defined power and the manipulation of social situations — even using less-than-virtuous means — as key leader attributes?
questions.explanation: Machiavelli, in The Prince, prescribed slyness and the use of less-than-virtuous means to gain power when virtuous means were inadequate.

questions.q: In the evolution of Organizational Behaviour, who propounded 'Division of labour and Work specialization' in 'The Wealth of Nations' (1776)?
questions.explanation: Adam Smith proposed a new organizational structure based on division of labour and work specialization in The Wealth of Nations (1776).

questions.q: Who is referred to as the 'real father of modern management' and defined the 14 principles of management?
questions.explanation: Henry Fayol, the 'real father of modern management', defined the universal functions of managers and the 14 principles of management.

questions.q: According to Stephen P. Robbins, Organizational Behaviour investigates the impact that which three things have on behaviour within organizations?
questions.explanation: Robbins defines OB as the study of the impact that individuals, groups and structure have on behaviour within organizations, to improve effectiveness.

questions.q: In organizational structure, 'span of control' refers to:
options: The total number of subordinates over whom a manager has authority
questions.explanation: Span of control is the total number of subordinates over whom a manager has authority; formalization, centralization and complexity are other structural concepts.

questions.q: The four functions of management are:
questions.explanation: Management is the process of planning, organizing, leading and controlling an organization's resources to increase effectiveness.

questions.q: Aptitude differs from ability in that aptitude:
options: Is the current capacity to perform a task
Represents a person's potential/capability of learning something
questions.explanation: Aptitude is a person's potential capability of learning something, whereas ability is the existing capacity (knowledge and skills) to perform tasks now.

questions.q: In the Big Five personality model, which trait describes being responsible, dependable, persistent and achievement-oriented?
questions.explanation: Conscientiousness captures being organized, dependable, responsible and self-disciplined — a good predictor of job performance.

questions.q: A person who believes that what happens to them is a result of fate, chance or luck has a(n):
questions.explanation: External locus of control = believing outcomes are due to fate/luck/others; internal locus = believing one's own behaviour determines outcomes.

questions.q: Type A individuals are best described as:
options: Intensely competitive, impatient, with a chronic sense of time urgency
questions.explanation: Type A individuals have an intense desire to achieve, are competitive, impatient and have a sense of time urgency; Type B are relaxed and easy-going.

questions.q: Perception is defined as:
options: Simply what one sees with the eyes
A process by which individuals organize and interpret sensory impressions to give meaning to their environment
A fixed, objective record of reality
questions.explanation: Perception is the cognitive process by which individuals organize and interpret sensory impressions to give meaning to their environment — so it is subjective.

questions.q: Judging someone on the basis of the group to which he or she belongs is which perceptual shortcut?
questions.explanation: Stereotyping is judging someone based on the group they belong to; the halo effect bases a general impression on a single characteristic.

questions.q: The Gestalt principle of 'closure' in perception means people:
options: Mentally fill in gaps/missing parts to make information a meaningful whole
Separate a figure from its background
questions.explanation: Closure is the mental process of filling in missing elements to form a meaningful whole; proximity, similarity and figure-ground are other Gestalt principles.

questions.q: How is a belief distinguished from an attitude?
options: Belief is purely emotional; attitude is factual
A belief is the cognitive component of an attitude — a hypothesis about the nature of objects — held more firmly than an opinion
An attitude is always written down
questions.explanation: A belief is an enduring organization of perceptions/cognitions — the cognitive component of attitude — and is held more firmly than a changeable opinion.

questions.q: Which of the following is an INFORMAL group?
options: A department created by the organization to handle customer complaints
A functional group with a superior-subordinate relationship
Members who share an interest in cricket and spend tea breaks together
A project task force appointed by the plant manager
questions.explanation: Informal groups emerge from members' interactions and common interests (e.g. a cricket-interest group), unlike formally created functional or task groups.

questions.q: In Tuckman's model of group development, which stage is characterised by intra-group conflict and resistance to the control the group imposes on individuality?
questions.explanation: Storming is the second stage, marked by intra-group conflict and power struggles over who will control the group.

questions.q: A self-managed team is one that:
options: Only shares information with no joint work
Takes on many responsibilities of their former supervisors — planning, scheduling, assigning tasks, and operating decisions
Uses only video conferencing to collaborate
questions.explanation: Self-managed teams (typically 10-15 people) take on supervisory responsibilities: planning/scheduling work, controlling pace, making operating decisions, even hiring.

questions.q: Quality circles are an example of which type of team?
questions.explanation: Quality circles — small groups meeting regularly to discuss and solve quality problems — are a form of problem-solving team.

questions.q: Hofstede's cultural dimension model was based on a study of employees at which company across 50+ countries?
questions.explanation: Hofstede studied IBM employees in more than 50 countries, allowing him to attribute patterns to national rather than company culture.

questions.q: A high Power Distance Index (PDI) country is one where:
options: Power is shared and widely dispersed
Society accepts an unequal, hierarchical distribution of power and people understand 'their place'
Supervisors and employees are treated as equals
There is no hierarchy at all
questions.explanation: High PDI means society accepts unequal, hierarchical power distribution; low PDI means flatter organizations where power is shared.

questions.q: In Hofstede's model, Individualism versus Collectivism refers to:
options: How society handles anxiety and uncertainty
The strength of the ties people have to others within their community
The distribution of roles between men and women
questions.explanation: The IDV dimension measures the strength of interpersonal ties — individualist cultures have weak ties beyond the core family, collectivist cultures demand group loyalty.

questions.q: Which Hofstede dimension describes how well people cope with anxiety and the desire to make life predictable and controllable?
questions.explanation: The Uncertainty Avoidance Index (UAI) describes how people cope with anxiety; high-UAI societies try to make life predictable and rule-bound.

questions.q: The Balance Theory of group formation (Newcomb) states that groups form when:
options: Individuals are attracted to one another because of similar/identical attitudes toward common objects or goals
Rewards exceed the costs of interaction
questions.explanation: Newcomb's Balance Theory holds that groups form when individuals share similar attitudes toward common objects or goals; Propinquity theory stresses geographical nearness.

questions.q: The relationship expressing a group's actual output is:
options: Group Productivity = Group Potential + Process Gain
Group Productivity = Group Potential − Process Loss
Group Productivity = Process Loss − Group Potential
questions.explanation: Group Productivity = Group Potential − Process Loss; process losses (e.g. coordination problems, social loafing) reduce the group's realized output.

questions.q: A 'reference group' is best defined as a group:
options: To which an individual would like to belong
Formed only by direct reporting relationships
Characterized by large size and no interaction
questions.explanation: A reference group is one to which a person would like to belong (and whose values they adopt), distinct from a membership group they actually belong to.

questions.q: Benne and Sheats' team MAINTENANCE role of 'Harmonizer' involves:
options: Mediating differences between members and relieving tension in conflict, often through humour
questions.explanation: The Harmonizer (a maintenance role) mediates disagreements and relieves tension; initiating/recording are task roles.

questions.q: Research identifies five dimensions of trust in high-performance teams. Which two are the most critical?
questions.explanation: The five trust dimensions are integrity, competence, consistency, loyalty and openness; integrity and competence are the most critical in judging trustworthiness.

questions.q: 'Social loafing' on a team refers to the tendency of individuals to:
options: Hide inside a group and coast on the group's effort because individual contributions can't be identified
questions.explanation: Social loafing is coasting on group effort because individual contributions aren't identified; high-performing teams counter it with individual and joint accountability.

questions.q: According to the notes, the best (most effective) work teams tend to be:
options: Small — typically fewer than about 10-12 members
questions.explanation: The best work teams are small (roughly 5-12, under a dozen); larger numbers struggle to develop cohesiveness, commitment and mutual accountability.

questions.q: The word 'communication' derives from the Latin 'communis', meaning:
questions.explanation: 'Communication' comes from the Latin 'communis' (common) — it refers to sharing/making common ideas, facts and understanding.

questions.q: In organizational communication, lateral communication (across chains of command) is carried out by people called:
questions.explanation: Those active in lateral communication are 'boundary spanners'; by accumulating information across units they gain power and status.

questions.q: In nonverbal communication, 'proxemics' is the study of:
options: The measurable physical/personal distance between people as they interact
questions.explanation: Proxemics studies personal space/distance (intimate, personal, social, public); oculesics is eye contact, chronemics is time, haptics is touch.

questions.q: 'Kinesics' refers to the interpretation of:
options: Body language — facial expressions, gestures and body movement
questions.explanation: Kinesics is body language — facial expressions, gestures and other physical movements that convey meaning.

questions.q: Which communication style stands up for one's own rights while maintaining respect for the rights of others?
questions.explanation: Assertive communication stands up for your rights while respecting others'; passive puts others first, aggressive violates others' rights.

questions.q: The upward-communication mechanism originally created in Scandinavia to receive and respond to employee complaints and allegations of injustice is the:
questions.explanation: The ombudsperson, originating in Scandinavia, receives and responds to employee inquiries, complaints and allegations of injustice, resolving issues quickly.

questions.q: Organizational culture is best defined as:
options: A system of shared assumptions, values and beliefs that signal appropriate and inappropriate behaviour
The org chart and reporting lines
questions.explanation: Organizational culture is a system of shared assumptions, values and beliefs that show members what behaviour is appropriate and inappropriate.

questions.q: In organizational culture, a 'counterculture' is a subgroup whose values:
options: Are in direct opposition to the dominant culture's values
Only add to the dominant values
questions.explanation: A counterculture's values are in opposition to the dominant culture; a subculture instead shares the core values while adding its own.

questions.q: In Schein's levels of organizational culture, which level is the most visible (behaviour, language, attire, décor)?
questions.explanation: Artifacts (behaviour, language, architecture, attire, décor) are the highly visible surface level; values are harder to see and basic assumptions are often unconscious.

questions.q: A 'strong' organizational culture is one that:
options: Has little agreement among employees on values
Is shared — most employees show consensus on and intensely hold the company's values
Relies on extensive bureaucracy and procedures
questions.explanation: A strong culture has values that are widely shared and intensely held (consensus); it can be an asset or liability depending on whether values fit the environment.

questions.q: What is the key difference between organizational culture and organizational climate (per Denison)?
options: Culture is the deep underlying structure (values, beliefs, assumptions); climate is the surface, observable practices/procedures and 'how it feels' to work there
Climate is permanent; culture is temporary
Culture applies only to new employees
questions.explanation: Denison: culture is the underlying structure embedded in values/beliefs/assumptions; climate is reflected in observable practices and is more temporary and perceivable.

questions.q: How do the notes distinguish employee morale from motivation?
options: Morale is a composite of feelings/attitudes/sentiments ('mobilization of sentiments'); motivation moves a person to action ('mobilization of energy')
Morale moves people to action; motivation is just a feeling
Motivation is only measurable, morale is not relevant
questions.explanation: Morale is a composite of feelings/attitudes (mobilization of sentiments), while motivation is the process that moves a person to action (mobilization of energy).

questions.q: Which is a recognised method for indirectly measuring employee morale?
options: Attitude/morale surveys and examining company records (absenteeism, turnover, grievances)
Counting the number of emails sent
questions.explanation: Morale is measured indirectly via observation, attitude/morale surveys, morale indicators (absenteeism, turnover, grievances) and suggestion boxes.

questions.q: Which group-leadership style is 'hands-off' — providing resources then stepping aside, remaining available to help only when the group asks?
questions.explanation: The laissez-faire (hands-off) style provides resources and lets members complete tasks with little direct involvement, assisting only when desired.

questions.q: Leadership perspectives generally fall into four main categories. Which is one of them?
questions.explanation: The four main categories are trait, situational (context-based), functional, and transformational leadership.

questions.q: In Hersey and Blanchard's Situational Leadership model, the 'Telling' (S1) style is best matched to which follower maturity level?
options: M1 (lack skills, knowledge or confidence; need specific direction)
questions.explanation: Telling (S1) — giving specific directions — matches M1 followers who lack the skills, knowledge or confidence and need external direction.

questions.q: In Hersey and Blanchard's model, the 'Delegating' (S4) style is characterised by:
options: Telling people exactly what to do
Focusing on relationships, relying on member expertise, and letting members take responsibility for decisions while monitoring progress
Selling the message to gain compliance
questions.explanation: Delegating (S4) focuses on relationships, relies on members' professional expertise, lets them take responsibility for decisions, and monitors progress — suited to M4.

questions.q: Functional leadership requires the leader to assess and balance which three types of needs?
options: Task needs, Team needs and Individual needs
questions.explanation: Functional leadership assesses Task, Team and Individual needs, devoting time and resources to each in priority order (task completion is highest priority but balanced).

questions.q: Who first introduced the concept of transformational leadership, describing the dynamic relationship between leader and followers?
questions.explanation: James MacGregor Burns first introduced transformational leadership; Bernard Bass later added its four key components.

questions.q: Which is one of Bass's four components of transformational leadership?
options: Inspirational Motivation (communicating a clear, compelling vision)
questions.explanation: Bass's four components are Intellectual Stimulation, Individualized Consideration, Inspirational Motivation and Idealized Influence.

questions.q: An 'emergent' leader is one who:
options: Is designated by an authority regardless of the group's wishes
Is elected or chosen by the group
Grows into the leadership role over time, often out of necessity, as the group looks to them
Has a formal title and corner office
questions.explanation: An emergent leader grows into the role out of necessity as group members look to them (e.g. the most experienced member), unlike appointed or democratically-elected leaders.

questions.q: The US Navy concept of 'deckplate leadership' means:
options: Leading only from the office via email
Getting out of the office and onto the deck/where the action is, interacting and learning the real challenges — balancing task and relationship
questions.explanation: Deckplate leadership means getting out of the office to where the work happens, interacting and learning the real challenges while balancing task and relationship.

questions.q: Ligon, Hunter and Mumford concluded that what makes a leader across contexts is an individual who can:
options: Be born with inherited aristocratic traits
In the presence of a crisis or challenge, formulate and implement a plan of action based on the context
questions.explanation: Their research concluded leadership is the ability to effectively formulate and implement a plan of action based on the context, especially in a crisis or challenge.
